review_notes: I read the whole file. I checked the simp-relevant weight lemmas in TreePolynomial.lean and TreePolynomialLists.lean. I also checked how other files in the Complexity directory discharge the same polynomial-evaluation goals, and I inspected the tree_poly macro. weight_prod, weight_nil and weight_cons are already @[simp], so the file has no competing rules or rewrite cycles that I could identify. I found no problem with the orientation of any existing lemma. The two findings are interface gaps, both stated without running Lean. First, the same long `simp only` list is copied into each polynomial bound proof. Second, insertStep and dedupStep have no equation lemmas, so proofs unfold them by `simp [insertStep,h]` or `change`. I did not recommend making weight_orderedInsert or weight_perm simp lemmas, because that would be only marginal benefit.

findings.declaration: polynomial_dedup / polynomial_orderedInsert / polynomial_insertionSort (repeated polynomial-evaluation simp set)
findings.problem: The same five-lemma `simp only` list is pasted into each polynomial-time bound proof. It appears at lines 62, 152 and 181 of this file, and again in TreePolynomialCollections, TreePolynomialArithmetic, TreePolynomialLists, TreePolynomialLoop and others. Each copy is the same hand-maintained normal form (evaluate the bound polynomial, split weight of pairs) that the proofs hand to `omega`. There is no named simp set or macro for it. `tree_poly` handles only the realizer-structure side. The list has to be retyped in every file, and the copies already drift: some add eval_one, eval_C or eval_comp, others omit weight_prod. Bare `simp` is not a substitute: it can also rewrite the weight and arithmetic terms before `omega` sees them.
findings.proposed_change: In TreePolynomial.lean, next to weight_prod, register a dedicated simp attribute with `register_simp_attr`, for example `tree_eval`. Tag it onto weight_prod, weight_cons and weight_nil, and onto Polynomial.eval_add, eval_mul, eval_ofNat, eval_X, eval_one and eval_C. Alternatively, define a small macro such as `tree_eval_simp` that expands to this `simp only` call. In this file, replace the three copies with that single call, e.g. `simp only [tree_eval]` followed by `omega`.
findings.benefit: The canonical normal form for these polynomial-bound goals is defined once. Proofs get shorter. A new Polynomial or weight evaluation lemma needs to be added in one place only, not in every copy.

findings.declaration: insertStep and dedupStep (no equation or simp lemmas for the case split)
findings.excerpt: have hs : insertStep r (b,(a,(bs,cs)))=(a,(b::bs,a::b::bs)) := by simp [insertStep,h]
findings.problem: insertStep and dedupStep are plain defs whose behaviour depends on a decidable test (`r x.2.1 x.1`, and `x.1∈x.2` for dedupStep). There are no equation lemmas for them. Every proof therefore unfolds the definition ad hoc. Examples are `simp [insertStep,h]` at lines 117 and 128 (restating the full result tuple each time), `simp [insertStep]` at lines 28 and 72, and `change weight (if a∈bs then bs else a::bs)≤_` at line 48, which relies on defeq. Passing the full definition to simp exposes the projection-heavy body `(x.2.1,(x.1::x.2.2.1,if …))` to the simplifier at every use. Callers also must restate the exact normal form.
findings.proposed_change: Add equation lemmas on constructor-form arguments. For insertStep: `insertStep r (b,(a,(bs,cs)))=(a,(b::bs,if r a b then a::b::bs else b::cs))`, plus the two hypothesis-guarded versions `insertStep_of_rel (h : r a b)` and `insertStep_of_not_rel (h : ¬ r a b)`. For dedupStep: `dedupStep (a,bs)=if a∈bs then bs else a::bs`, plus `dedupStep_of_mem` and `dedupStep_of_not_mem`. Mark the guarded versions @[simp]. Their hypotheses are discharged by simp, they do not loop, and each shrinks to one cons-form output. Then lines 117 and 128 become `by simp [h]` (or rw), and line 48 can `simp [dedupStep]` or `rw` instead of using `change`.
findings.benefit: The case analysis is stated once as rewrite rules, not re-derived with `simp [insertStep,h]` in every proof. Proofs no longer depend on definitional unfolding. The simp normal form of a step on a pair is predictable, so later lemmas about these folds are easier to write.
